subject: Vocabulary
description: Latin / French phrases used in English; high-hit SSC PYQ items

questions.stem: What does the Latin phrase 'STATUS QUO' mean?

options.option_text: A new beginning fresh and clean
Existing state of affairs (no change)
Conflict situation between two sides
Final decision authority of state

questions.explanation: STATUS QUO (Latin) = 'the state in which' = the existing state of affairs. 'Maintain status quo' = keep things as they are; don't change. 'Status quo ante' = the previous state (before something happened). Common in legal, diplomatic, political contexts. PYQ-favourite.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Without reasonable doubt
In good faith / genuine
Without any reservation
After careful examination

questions.explanation: BONA FIDE = 'in good faith' (Latin). Used to mean genuine, sincere, real. 'A bona fide claim' = genuine claim. 'Bona fide certificate' = genuine school/employment certificate. Antonym: MALA FIDE = bad faith. Other Latin pairs: prima facie (at first sight), de facto (in fact), de jure (in law), in toto (in total), pro rata (proportional), per capita (per head).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Final outcome of an event
Mode / method of operation
Initial planning of project
Authority of operating power

questions.explanation: MODUS OPERANDI (M.O.) = method of operating; way of working. Often used for criminals: 'the burglar's MO was to enter through windows'. Modus vivendi = mode/way of living (esp. compromise allowing two parties to coexist). Modus tollens / modus ponens = logical inference rules.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Peaceful protest of citizens
Sudden overthrow of government
Royal proclamation by king
Diplomatic agreement between states

questions.explanation: COUP D'ÉTAT (lit. 'stroke of state') — sudden, illegal overthrow of government, often by military. Commonly shortened to 'COUP'. Examples: Napoleon's coup (1799); various Latin America + Africa coups in 20th c.; Myanmar coup (2021). Other French phrases in English: COUP DE GRACE (= 'mercy stroke', the killing blow); BON VOYAGE (good journey); CARTE BLANCHE (full freedom); FAUX PAS (false step / social blunder); RENDEZVOUS (meeting); DEJA VU (already seen); NOUVEAU RICHE (newly rich); SAVOIR FAIRE (know how).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Recorded on video for archives
In private (closed-door hearing)
On TV broadcast for public
In open court session viewing

questions.explanation: IN CAMERA = 'in the chamber' (Latin) = privately, in chambers; closed to public. Used in legal contexts: 'the case was heard in camera' = closed-door hearing (often for sensitive matters: rape, child abuse, national security). NOT related to photography 'camera' (although same Latin root — 'chamber'). PYQ-favourite legal Latin.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: After much consideration here
From the very beginning
In the present moment now
At the future date later

questions.explanation: AB INITIO = 'from the beginning' (Latin). 'The contract was void ab initio' = invalid from the very start. 'I'll start ab initio' = from scratch. Other 'ab' phrases: AB OVO = 'from the egg' (from origin, similar meaning); AB EXTRA = from outside.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: What does 'PRIMA FACIE' (Latin) mean in legal context?

options.option_text: Final and conclusive proof here
On first appearance / first sight
After deep investigation finally
Without any reasonable doubt

questions.explanation: PRIMA FACIE = 'on the face of it' / 'at first sight'. Suggests apparent truth, not yet proven. 'A prima facie case' = enough evidence to proceed; not yet proof. Compare with 'beyond reasonable doubt' (criminal — much higher standard) + 'preponderance of evidence' (civil — > 50%). Also: prima donna = leading female opera singer; prima ballerina; primary; primer.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: What does the French phrase 'CARTE BLANCHE' mean when used in English?

options.option_text: A task already completed before others could raise objections
An official request or formal order issued by an authority
Complete, unconditional freedom to act as one wishes
An unavoidable event or situation entirely beyond one's control

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'Carte blanche' literally means 'blank card' in French, implying total freedom to act without restriction. Option A describes 'fait accompli', and Option D describes 'force majeure' — both common confusions within this group of French phrases tested in SSC/IBPS vocabulary sections.

questions.stem: What is the precise meaning of the Latin expression 'PER SE' in formal academic or legal writing?

options.option_text: By itself, inherently or intrinsically considered
On behalf of another person acting as a proxy
In the same manner and form as done previously
According to the established custom or legal rule

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'Per se' means 'by itself' or 'in itself' — e.g., 'the act is not illegal per se'. Option B describes 'per procurationem (per pro)', and Option D resembles 'de jure'. These are frequently confused with 'per se' in reading-comprehension passages on SSC and IBPS papers.

questions.stem: In civil proceedings, a court issues an 'EX PARTE' order. Which situation CORRECTLY describes this scenario?

options.option_text: Both parties are heard equally before the bench passes its order
A senior judge reviews a junior court's verdict on appeal
The case is jointly decided by a full bench of three or more judges
One party proceeds and obtains relief without the other being present

questions.explanation: D is correct: 'Ex parte' means 'from one party' — the order is granted on one side's application without the other party being notified or heard. Option A describes an 'audi alteram partem' proceeding, which is the direct opposite principle. Options B and C describe appellate and full-bench procedures, which are unrelated.

questions.stem: Which phrase BEST defines the Latin expression 'SINE QUA NON' as used in official and academic English?

options.option_text: Added voluntarily but not strictly required by any rule
An absolute and indispensable prerequisite for something
Done simultaneously alongside another primary obligation
Officially ratified by a competent legal or state authority

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Sine qua non' literally means 'without which not' — something so essential that it cannot be omitted. Option A is the opposite meaning (voluntary/non-essential) and is a deliberate trap. Option D echoes 'de jure' or 'ratified', which is unrelated. Examiners test this in HR, policy, and legal reading-comprehension passages.

questions.stem: The French expression 'VIS-À-VIS' is commonly found in formal reports and government documents. It is used to mean:

options.option_text: In relation to, or as compared with, a specific thing
Directly opposing and fundamentally contradicting the main argument
A preliminary agreement concluded informally before final settlement
A concluding summary or annex appended at the end of a document

questions.explanation: A is correct: 'Vis-à-vis' literally means 'face to face' in French but in formal usage means 'in relation to' or 'compared with' — e.g., 'India's trade surplus vis-à-vis China'. Option B sounds plausible but describes 'contra' or 'versus'. Option C describes a memorandum of understanding (MoU), a separate concept.

questions.stem: A Supreme Court judgment reads: 'The petitioner cited, inter alia, a violation of Article 21.' What role does 'INTER ALIA' play in this sentence?

options.option_text: It signals an exclusive focus, limiting the argument to a single ground
It indicates that every party to the case has raised the identical point
It conveys that the Article 21 violation was one of several grounds raised
It qualifies the claim as filed without prejudice to all other remedies

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'Inter alia' means 'among other things' — the petitioner raised Article 21 among multiple grounds, not exclusively. Option A is the precise opposite and is the most common trap since students confuse 'inter alia' with 'inter se' (among themselves). Option D describes 'without prejudice', a distinct legal phrase used to protect settlement negotiations.

questions.stem: A plaintiff in a tort case successfully invokes 'RES IPSA LOQUITUR'. Which scenario BEST justifies its application?

options.option_text: The defendant signs a written admission of fault before the hearing begins
A surgical sponge is discovered inside a patient after a routine operation
A contract is declared void because both parties shared a mutual mistake
The plaintiff's lawyer submits independent documentary evidence of negligence

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'Res ipsa loquitur' means 'the thing speaks for itself' — it applies when the very occurrence of an event implies negligence, sparing the plaintiff from proving each element separately. A surgical sponge left inside a patient is the classic illustration. Option A eliminates the need for the doctrine since admission removes the evidentiary burden. Option D involves external proof, which is exactly what this doctrine is designed to avoid.
